review_text_raw:
I have a confession.

I like goofy fake hacking scenes in movies.

I know it's not indicative of "actual" hacking, and as a programmer I should probably be a little miffed at how unrealistic they make the whole thing seem. But I don't care! I love it anyway.

Hacknet promised to give me that kind of feeling, and like Uplink before it, it kinda did. It's a puzzle game where your tools are 'hacking programs' and your problems relate to breaking into computers and grabbing info, deleting info, or causing chaos.

It works well, and it reveals just how satisfying it is to solve software problems, even when it's heavily abstracted and simplified.

But my biggest problem with Hacknet is that it never really takes that next step into something greater than a simplified hacking game. Toward the end of the game there's a distinct feeling of "That was it?"

Want to hack an SSH port? Then use SSHportHack.exe. Want to hack an FTP port? Then use FTPportHack.exe. The entire game is like this. For each problem or situation there's almost always exactly one answer, and there are few opportunities to feel clever. 

In some ways the game actually feels unfinished. Many computers you hack into contain generically named folders that are either empty or have snippets of IRC conversations from Bash.org. The game is set in modern times, yet your computer only has ~800mb of RAM and you can never upgrade it. The UI for selecting systems to hack into is an absolute nightmare.

There are even mechanics that don't seem to actually...exist? For example, a big deal is made about deleting your logs and leaving no trace behind - a classic hacking trope - yet I never once saw any consequences for forgetting. I eventually just stopped clearing logs and it never was a problem

As I said, I like Hackers-style hacking. It's fun and goofy and still scratches the same itch as actual hacking. Hacknet gets close, but its far too shallow and misses the mark.

review_text_raw:
The gameplay basically consists of nothing but navigating folders. There's no coding to be done, no puzzles to be solved. 
All you'll do is connect to "computers" (folders), run a program that magically "hacks" your way into them, scan for more "computers" to "hack", rinse and repeat. It is mind numbing and repetitive.

I kept playing because I thought surely something interesting must happen eventually, but I was wrong. The most challenging problem you'll have to solve is writing down a password to use on a locked folder.

If you want to feel like a super smart hacker without having to put in any actual effort, you might like this game. If you were looking for a real puzzle game, then look elsewhere.

review_text_raw:
"Real Hacking
Based on actual UNIX commands, Hacknet focuses on real hacking, not the Hollywood-style version of it. This creates a truly immersive experience and puts players right in the thick of trying to break through the firewalls."

Blatant lies. Hacknet is straight up Hollywood hacking. The terminal is a simplistic cross-breed between bash and cmd.exe. It puts you in the role of a script kiddy, who "hacks" systems by observing which ports are open on the target machine and running the corresponding hacking program by typing its name and a port number (e.g. "FTPHack 21"). Once you're in, your job is to either snoop through some files for a password, to download files, or to delete them using basic terminal skills. You're supposed to cover your tracks by deleting logs, but it rarely matters. The same thing, over and over, no brains required. There's no sense you're accomplishing anything of value, nor of any consequence to yourself or others.

It's an insult to anyone with more than a surface-level understanding of network security, as challenging to a puzzle gamer as 50 consecutive games of Tic-tac-toe, and isn't even that interesting in terms of Hollywood hacking simulations. It's on par with a budding game developer's first project, not something worth spending $10 to $24 on. If you want an intellectual challenge (Hollywood setting, but real problem-solving), check out Zachtronics (Exapunks, Shenzhen I/O, TIS-100).

That said, Hacknet does have a few high points. The music is pretty great. The Labyrinths DLC is slightly less mediocre, but isn't worth the regular $7 price point on top of the base game's $10. If everything was like the DLC's final mission — which unexpectedly drops you into a timed, high-stakes situation with dire consequences — this might actually be a decent game. As is, though, it's just a bland waste of money.

Final Update (3):
Seeing as the dev doesn't seem to give a damn anymore about providing the patches necessary to have the game work as advertised in a timely manner, I won't check on it or update the review any further.
Maybe the game will someday be what it should've been from day 1, but 3 weeks early access quality for a full release isn't acceptable.

-------------------------------------------------------------

Sadly, this has to be a [b]not recommended[/b] review.
The reason for this is the apparent lack of quality control before release. See details below.

First off, the concept is great. I really want to love this game for it's concept. It is basically a much better version of Uplink.
Now, is it realistic from a hacking point of view? No. But that's a good thing, because realistic hacking scenarios would be pretty boring for a game. The concepts are taken from the real world and simplified/modified to make an interesting game.

It is simple at first and doesn't get too difficult while still providing some challenges and a nice storyline. 

That being said, while the game could be a 9/10, game-breaking bugs currently make it at most a 4/10.

Here are some that I've encountered so far:
- You are able to take multiple contracts at some point, but doing so will prevent further progression due to the quest completion system being bugged.
- Using multiple profiles is inconsistent, you can't be sure that your savegame remains the way it was
- Game supports windowed mode but crashes regularly if you focus on another window
- Loss of all savegames - this is a big one. The last time the aforementioned crash occured, I've lost all of my saves.

The last bug on this list is the main reason this review has come to a not recommended conclusion and the others severely contributed.
If any beta testing would've been done, such a list of game-breaking bugs wouldn't exist.

Update 1: After the most recent patch promised a solution  to "many issues that were causing people to lose save files" I've decided to start a new profile. Did some work, saved session and exited the game normally. And alas, as I started the game again today there were no accounts and my save_accountsMeta.xml was gone. Again. This is clearly getting ridiculous and I wouldn't expect a solution any time soon, the dev will probably need a few weeks to figure out the issues with Steam API/Cloud saves etc.

Update 2: Since apparently fixing the savegame issues within a reasonable amount of time isn't happening, I have to say this is close to false advertising. The game should be tagged early access if the amount of issues is still that extensive after two patches. This is the sort of behaviour I'd expect from large companies that simply don't give a sh*t anymore, not form an indie dev trying to make his name. I hope the dev learns some things from this failed release, one of them being that you shouldn't release a game full of bugs when you're too busy being at conventions after the release and don't have time to fix the issues.

Don't get me wrong: everyone makes mistakes and stuff like that can happen. But that doesn't change the fact that as a customer I kinda feel cheated, since there's a reason I don't buy early access and this time the product isn't of higher quality.
Again, once the major bugs are fixed and solutions for the existing issues are presented, I'll gladly give this game a recommendation.

review_text_raw:
I’m not entirely sure what to think about this game. I feel like this game had the potential to be a lot more interesting than it turned out to be. I did have fun with this game and thought some of the missions were interesting. But, I can’t really figure out what this game is trying to be and I came away with the feeling that this game isn’t really finished. 

In terms of hacking and the operating system, it’s fairly weak and, at times, frustrating. The hacking programs you run are basically magic in terms of how powerful they are. They work on anything and require no modification based on the target. The challenge comes from managing your bizarre computer’s memory system and timing attacks to avoid the hollywood-style ‘tracing’. The simplified hacking mechanics aren’t a bad thing, I think. Real hacking elements would make the game extremely complicated, tedious, and boring. 

But, that aside, there are weird limitations on what you can do and what exists in the world. The operating system commands you run are unix-based, but quickly get frustrating to use for anyone familiar with *nix command lines. Autocompletion and wildcards are inconsistent (‘rm *’ works but not ‘rm file_*’). There is no cp (copy), mkdir, rmdir, rsync, or recursion-supported operations. There isn’t even a text editor of any kind, opting for a bizarre ‘replace’ to replace strings in a given file. This just causes more frustration than anything as folders become cluttered and basic OS actions can't be done.

As for the world, hacking into servers and snooping around is fun… to a point. You can read other people’s emails, deface websites, and steal files, which is fun! Then you realize that most of the files you discover are copy-pasted bash.org quotes or filler files which you can’t do anything with. Also, you’re strongly told early on to remove the log files you leave behind when hacking a server, but I’ve yet to find an instance where there are any consequences for not doing so outside of one mission. Finally, and probably my biggest problem, is that you’re pretty much the only active user on the entire internet. You’ll never accidentally encounter another hacker when breaking into a server and you’ll (with one exception) never find log files or evidence of dynamic activity from anyone else on the internet. The world is completely static, apart from a few scripted events. Maybe if there were random encounters or events with other hackers where both of you have the ability to hack each other and other servers, the world wouldn’t feel so static and empty and it would keep you on your toes a bit more. 

The investigation and puzzle aspects of the game are interesting. But, the large number of typos,  grammar mistakes (not sure if these two are intentional or not), and questionable writing can be distracting and confusing. That said, I still had fun. There are times where the missions can be very interesting and even disturbing. And, occasionally, there are times where you have to be clever to solve a puzzle or find a missing piece of information. But, those events are far and few in between. Most of the ‘contracts’ start to feel tedious pretty quickly.

I hate that there is no option inbetween the thumbs up and down, because I think the game is still fun. But, comparing how much I liked to how much I didn’t like, I have to give it a thumbs down. This game has great ideas, it just hasn’t fleshed them out enough.

PREFACE: I only played this game for one hour, and this may be a biased review, but so far I didn't see anything worth pursuing. The game may get interesting further down, but it just didn't pique my interesting so far.

This game does way too much hand holding to be enjoyable. If you're a casual gamer who wants to get the feeling that you're a cool hacker, go for it, but if you want any actual challenge, this game is not for you.

The whole game is just reading long emails trying to get the important information, then running the same sequence of commands over and over for every challenge. Every time they want to make it harder, they just add one more command to this sequence and repeat the same process.

There was very little problem solving or experimenting happening, which to me is what hacking is all about. Trying things out yourself and learning new tools. Not someone telling you what to do each step of the way.

The terminal interface was neat and the soundtrack was banging, but the game was just too bland and repetitive to be enjoyable.

review_text_raw:
This is an OK game. I wouldn't go as far as to compare it to either Uplink or the Street Hacker series simply because it feels more like a demo when compared to them. The execution and gameplay is shallow and naive. It's plagued by many basic design issues and most of the missions are just boring, repetitive, and feel more like a chore rather than a challenge.

My biggest gripes are:
-boring, repetitive and easy missions. Only 2 interesting missions stand out, the final Bit one, and the online pacemaker one.
-no sense of urgency or challenge. If you get caught hacking, that's just a reload to last checkpoint. No point in deleting any logs the way Uplink makes sure that you do. Uplink kept you on your toes because getting caught meant absolute game over!
-Badly designed UI. The workstation "map" is a cluttered mess especially as you move closer towards the end. Nodes are being randomly generated and the ones closest to the edge of the screen have their hover information cut off. How that ever went past the testers, I do not know!
-Weird writing, bad grammar, spelling mistakes, juvenile jokes scattered here and there. The ending was incredibly cheesy and anti-climactic.

Not a bad game to get on sale. But this is no Uplink for sure. The tagline shouldn't be "if you liked Uplink, you'll love this!" It's more the other way around because now I definitely feel like going back and replaying Uplink for the zillionth time! :)

review_text_raw:
Good: 
[list]
    [*]the command line UI is accurate, and makes you feel a lot like a real hacker.
    [*]nice music
    [*]lots of little easter eggs
    [*]technically very accurate (uses correct port numbers, IP addresses, and more)
[/list]

Bad: 
[list]
   [*]core gameplay is extremely repetitive and time consuming (which is an awful combination)
[/list]

The core gameplay of Hacknet revolves around you, a hacker, who can run several different programs to hack into a server and complete some task for a client. For example, hacking into the fried chicken chain CFC server and stealing the list of 11 secret herbs and spices.

It's an interesting concept to start with, however the game falls extremely short in that the gameplay never evolves into anything that is challenging or involves meaningful decision making. 

Hacking each server in the entire game is exactly the same. That is no exaggeration. You literally do the exact same 3-7 things for each server you encounter in order to hack into it. And the worst part about this process is that the "hacking" requires no user interaction. You simply wait 1-2 minutes for the hacking programs to finish, and then you complete whatever task you were assigned to do on the server.

At no point do you need to make any in game decisions when hacking. At no point do you have any decision to make that can affect the gameplay. And that's really where it all falls apart for me. What am I really doing in this game? Because the game really lacks in the feeling of accomplishment.

I can completely understand how this gameplay can appeal to people who want to feel like a hacker, because the game definitely hits the mark in that regard. But once you get past that, you realise there is very little "gameplay" to be had. It just feels like a demo.

This might just be the 10 years since launch, or my actual experience with computers, but the gameplay loop feels a bit off (pun not intended) for me. The tutorial got me curious enough with the plot to get through, but there is no substance in the base game. Haven't played the DLC, not interested.

If you are into looking at hacker-looking interfaces and typing the same half a dozen commands over and over (tab complete and up key for history available), you will enjoy it. If you want anything that is anymore puzzling than following clear instructions, look elsewhere.

Basically: 1- open an email, 2- click email attachments for a target IP and maybe add a mission summary note to the screen, 3- click a button to connect to said IP and click another button to Probe the system, 4- run the same 2-5 commands on the same list of ports, 5- browse the filesystem to either find or place a file at mostly the same folders, 6- erase all logs and disconnect, 7- repeat. That's it. The game has a simplified terminal emulator missing a few basic features but fine, you can mostly use it to get things done instead of the GUI except when emailing (mostly). review_text_raw:
The game design works at first, and there are timed missions when you really get into the action – musics do their job. You have kind of a sense of accomplishment as you get your hands on more "hacking" tools and get to face bigger challenges. There is quite a lot of humorous content on the side – not in the main story! – and that's appreciated because it's not far from being a text game.

But that's about all the nice things I can think about this game. Pretty soon, you reach its limits and the sense of accomplishment fades away. If you have no feeling for IT stuff, you may get lost pretty fast. But if you're too much into it, the game mechanisms are very disappointing. The main idea was good, but the execution rather bad. If you're still curious, I'd suggest to buy it on sale.

The difficulty relies on: 1. The cryptic aspect of computers – you'd better know the basics about file system and console ;  2. Timed challenges ; 3. Finding little bits of information (user name, password, IP...) here and there among text in files and mail ; 4. Systematically scan the targets in all ways possible. That's not something that keeps one entertained for long.

The console, which you use a lot, is rather rudimentary. At the very least it should have felt like a real one and at least to go smoothly when you type. The cursor is glitchy, not always showing where it actually is. Key pushes may be repeated when hold a few microseconds too long. The number of commands is very limited. They are sometimes buggy when not used as intended. Managing the in-game files is pretty tedious, there are no commands for creating/deleting directories. There is no way to make scripts or shortcuts. At best you can rename the executables. By the way, having "exe" files on a Linux simulation is an heresy.

The graphic interface lacks functionalities too. It would be great if you could move and resize the panels, especially the one for the "netmap" which gets pretty packed and hard to read after a while. You may find an in-game executable which helps a little bit with that. Also content will overflow from panels when too big. Why no copy/paste available?!? It would have been so useful. I grew tired of retype every user name, password and IP. Plus there are some links that are meant to be open in a real browser (as eater eggs only).

The game mechanisms are very limited. Some special missions or events break the monotony, but the player are not prepared for them either. [spoiler]For instance you are not likely to be able to defend your computer against other hackers.[/spoiler] The hacking tools are also limited in number, in versions and they almost all work in the same way. Missions are quite alike, and you're doing the same dull things over, and over, and over...

They tried to make up for it with the game story, but it turns out to be a bit déjà vu, corny, and even a bit predictable.

Two alternatives would have been preferable for making such a game:
— Either make it more approachable, even less realistic but with a more pleasant game design. Then it would need hacking to be more like puzzles.
— Or make a game for nerds, where the in-game computers can be configured, where files matter, with better console commands and executables, even maybe some scripts to edit.

Even though I enjoyed some moments of Hacknet, overall it is a very repetitive experience even just at 4 hours total. The player is presented with many hacking missions that basically have two parts: Break into a computer, and do something in it. The breaking into is exactly identical for all computers which gets old fast. Once in the system, the objectives are varied but mostly cosmetic, i.e copy files, read text to get info, etc. Only a couple missions have real puzzles. 

In general the game just felt very shallow compared to other terminal simulators with more gimmicks, or with other hacking games like bitburner.

review_text_raw:
It is difficult to make a game that captures the feel of hacking. A hacker is successful because he has a large body of knowledge to pull from. He tries a thousand different things before something works.

Making an exciting game about hacking is like making an exciting game about coming up with new mathematical theorems. 

Hacknet is far more fun that I expected, but that isn't saying much. You are given four or five scripts to run with various levels of time pressure. There is a lot of good flavor, being able to customize your UI, using a simplified UNIX, and accessing system files.

Sadly, the gameplay wasn't enough to keep me playing and the story, while interesting, wasn't original enough to carry the game.

For a more detailed review of this and other Steam games I bought for cheap, check out my blog:

review_text_raw:
I hoped this game would be a spiritual successor to Uplink maybe with a little bit more realism. Unfortunately the game falls short of that aspiration.

First of all, it's not any more realistic than Uplink. While you get to use real Unix commands, you don't use them in a very similar way to the real thing. Have no illusion, this game will not teach you anything useful in real life. There's nothing wrong with making your hacking sim game a little over the top with fancy animations and misused tech lingo, but it's not what I expected.

Where the game really fails to live up to Uplink, however, is depth. Remember how Uplink had news bulletins reporting on your mischief, other active hackers taking assignments and getting arrested when you rat on them, multiple banks with multiple accounts wiring funds to each other, and a stock market where you could watch your victim corporations suffer losses after you hack and destroy their mainframes? You will find nothing like this in Hacknet. All you get it a lot of random IRC logs pasted from bash.org and some personal files and emails that are not written in a breathtaking way.

Is it fun? Yeah, especially if it's your first game of this kind. There's a thrill in accessing systems and files you shouldn't be looking at and there's even an overarching plot that's encouraging you to keep playing, but it all lacks depth, gameplay-wise, story-wise and writing-wise.

review_text_raw:
I have never left a review here in on steam for anything....that in itself should make you appreciate just how strongly I feel about what I am about to say and just how absolutely and unequivocally true what I am about to say really is.

Let's start from the positives.....actually positive:
The graphics are OK....along with the music it does create an atmosphere appropriate to the setting of the game.
That's it.

READ THIS BEFORE YOU BUY:
1) The game is essentially a mishap collection of dubiously formatted XML files, along with the main executable of the game which is obviously just a parser along with the graphics engine (presumably). Although it is possible to play the game normally, I guarantee that you will soon waste your time trying to "fix" the myriad of issues that arise from the poor structure of the gameplay itself (more on that later) See my play time? 87 hours? Most of it has been spent scouring the internet on ways to fix broken missions, enable progression through other parts of the story, etc.
2)There are several limits to and aspects of the basic design that make NO sense. For example, yes, you can use a "terminal" with a few commands to progress through the game. These commands include options to open and close your actual CD tray (wow, how ARG of the author--when was the last time anybody used the CD tray for anything? when was the last time anybody saw a computer with an actual CD drive ???). HOWEVER IT IS IMPOSSIBLE TO CREATE OR DELETE DIRECTORIES IN YOUR IN-GAME COMPUTER, NOR CREATE FILES..That's right....as crazy as it sounds, you can't even copy files on your own machine. The only way to create files is downloading them from somewhere else and then renaming them if you want to "fake" a simple copy command....but yes, if you want a game that opens your CD tray by all means, stop reading this now and buy the game. The terminal itself has no ability to scroll up, which sometimes means you need to retrace your steps if you forgot to jot some key piece of information down.
3)There is no hardware upgrade system, which means your hacking machine is what it is from beginning to end. It doesn't really matter for the most part, as the speed of the operations you perform in the game is largely dependent on your own ability and response time (that's the main game mechanic). However RAM is kind of important, because that's what all your hacking tools consume to run, as expected. The problem is that if you, for example have the notes app open with passwords and information about your current mission (thus avoiding the aforementioned backtracking in point 2) , you will run out of memory pretty quickly...forcing you to run programs one at a time and wishing you could actually make money in this game to buy more than 1 GB of ram (lol...seriously...just lol).
4)You can only accept 1 mission at a time (WHY...JUST WHY?!???!). This may not seem a big issue, but it is what literally breaks the game again and again. This ridiculous limitation means that you can't complete all the missions offered in the game because no matter what you do as you progress through the story the game forces you to move on and leave the unfinished missions behind, never to be played. The only way to get past this is to go and edit your save game (you guessed it, an XML file) in order to make it possible to complete some missions (this fix doesn't always work btw). This becomes a huge problem close to the end of the story. Without spoiling anything, you end up having two missions to do, and it seems that it doesn't matter the order you do them in, but if you choose wrong a subsequent mission will be skipped entirely (it is one of the most notorious bugs of the game) and you will miss part of the narrative and context. Seriously, if you are thinking of buying this game, in order to enjoy the story as it was meant to be played, you should first look up what I have just told you and figure out which mission you should do first when you get to that juncture, or be prepared to restart the whole game if you mess up (unbelievable).
5)The least the author could've done was to include a save management system, but of course, there is none. If you want to make sure you don't have to restart the game in case something gets screwed up (see above) you must manually backup your savegame file, and you have to be careful too...because although the game doesn't autosave normally it will autosave in certain circumstances, barely warning you that this has been done.
6)Although the game never crashes, there are a few technical bugs that wouldn't even be a problem if not for everything that i mentioned above. When working with the terminal, using the arrow keys to edit a command sometimes doesn't work properly, and there are a few other such things (sometimes, for example, you have to hack a computer twice because although you were able to hack in the first time, the game doesn't register it). There are also a few grammar mistakes that again, not really important on its own but if added to all of the above, it's just the "cherry" on top that you don't want...especially from a paid game, however cheap it is. 
7) There is a ranking system, but it doesn't work. No matter how many missions you complete and how high your rank is according to the success emails you get at the end of each completed mission, you are still the last on the list, with 0 points. It's annoying. Suggestion to the author: if a feature is too hard/you are to lazy to implement...don't include it, especially if it has no bearing on the gameplay whatsoever. It is pretty disappointing to reach the end of the game and see that in the eyes of your hacking faction you are still a newb. 

Now....I get it, it's an indie game...what did I expect? Well I expected something a little more functional. As a software developer myself I understand a few of the choices the author made, but sill...there are some laps in basic human logic that are beyond me. For example, it is obvious that is technically more difficult to write an "open world" style game as opposed to a linear game play experience. That's why the player is allowed to play one mission at a time. I really get it. What I don't get is if a linear game is what you wanted to code...THEN DO NOT OFFER CHOICES TO THE PLAYER THAT YOUR GAME IS UNABLE TO SUPPORT AND FORCE HIM/HER/THEY TO START OVER!!!
I also understand that is hard to test a piece of software by yourself, I have done it as my main occupation for many years. A few bugs are bound to crop up...but hey...IN THE CREDITS THERE ARE MENTIONED A WHOLE SLEW OF TESTERS...what the heck did they test exactly? Seriously...I want to see what test cases they ran on this....

I would ask for a refund...but hey if didn't get my 60 bucks back from CD Projekt RED for Cyberprank 2077 I certainly won't ask the 5 bucks i spent on this (i got the DLC too). Go ahead, enjoy your Starbucks latte on me.  
According to the author, this game started out as a 48h game jam project and was later refined for 2 and a half years to become what's on steam now. 2/3 YEARS??!?!?! THIS IS WHAT YOU COME UP WITH? I think the best definition of this game is just that....a barely interesting project  hurriedly cobbled together  for a 48h game jam event.

tl;dr; Do yourself a favor and buy Uplink Elite, which is obviously what this game wanted to be and failed...miserably. I'd be willing to gift Uplink to the author as well so that he can see how a game like this SHOULD be made.

I guess that if a hacking OS was developed in real life, it may actually be this easy, but in reality now hacking is way more difficult, complicated and sometimes more fun than this.

I came to experience a story, play a game, be something and someone else for a while, not to actually do hacker work. This is not a game I hate. However, much like that TIS-100 game, I was left completely clueless as to how to proceed, though nowhere near as quickly, thanks to an actual tutorial and being able to play a little bit of the game before getting stuck, as well as a help menu listing commands. As a child in the 80s, I spent a fair amount of time using DOS to find files, modify them, etc., and in college, I used UNIX for a semester, scoring an A. There isn't a day that goes by where I don't use a PC, unless something really weird happens, like a blackout. Therefore, I was more than a little surprised when I got so hopelessly dumbfounded by this game. Granted, this game is far classier than TIS-100.

This game actually has music, and it's quite nice, while TIS-100 had none that I found. TIS-100's manual was difficult to understand and quite daunting, while Hacknet is far more user friendly, and really appears to have a story and more purpose to it. That said, the game left me confused and stuck when I came upon a firewall. The game never covered how to deal with firewalls in the tutorial. I tried running a program I had just downloaded from another computer in-game, which let me access one port, but I couldn't access any of the other ports. I used every page of help to look up commands that could help me, and analyzing the firewall brought up a wall of letters and numbers that didn't seem to do anything, and selecting to "solve" the firewall didn't do anything, either. I checked every computer I had access to and found nothing else that could help me.

If I'm stuck this early in, checking a walkthrough or asking for help online will likely lead to me continuing my confused wandering without learning anything within the game itself. I should not have to rely on the Internet to learn how to play a game for fun...

I'm disappointed in the game, but only because I liked what I saw when the game was presenting things in a way that cleverly educates the player, but then it throws you a problem early-game that no amount of searching within the game itself appears to turn up a solution. The point where it figuratively drops you in the deep end of the digital pool with a cyber-anchor tied to your feet is where I lose any ability to appreciate the game beyond that point.

It's also entirely possible I lack the mental faculties to interact with this digital gaming experience in a fulfilling manner. If that's the case, then so be it, but I must represent the "mentally deficient" population and state that I do not recommend this game as a result.

review_text_raw:
Cool Concept, But It Couldn’t Keep Me Hooked

Hacknet starts strong. The idea of diving into a terminal-based hacking sim with a mysterious narrative hook is instantly appealing, especially if you’re into cyberpunk aesthetics or want to feel like a digital detective. At first, typing out real commands and navigating the virtual systems feels immersive and fresh. But that feeling didn’t last long for me.

The main problem is how quickly the novelty wears off. After a couple of missions, the gameplay loop becomes repetitive — scan, probe, crack, read a few emails, rinse and repeat. There’s little variety or meaningful evolution in the mechanics. You’re not solving clever puzzles so much as going through the motions of the same routine over and over.

The story, while intriguing in concept, never really grabbed me. It’s told in fragments through logs and emails, but it lacks emotional weight or urgency. I never felt particularly invested in the characters or their motivations — and a lot of the writing just felt flat.

On top of that, there are some pacing issues. Some tasks feel tedious and drawn out, while others jump ahead abruptly. And if you’re not already familiar with basic command-line structure, the early learning curve can feel more frustrating than fun.

I really wanted to like Hacknet. It nails the aesthetic and tone, and I respect the ambition. But the shallow gameplay and underwhelming story made it feel more like a tech demo than a fully satisfying experience.

review_text_raw:
I feel slightly bad giving this game a negative review given that I enjoyed most of the time I spent playing it, but I honestly can't recommend it.

The positives are more than adequately covered in other reviews, but for completeness: It does a solid job of recreating the Hollywood hacker fantasy, with hacks and counter-hacks, proxies, firewalls, trace countdowns, and all that good stuff. The story is nicely paced, with plenty of humour and knowing pop-culture references as you move from small-time nuisance hacks to big-time corporate takedowns. And there is a mildly satisfying payoff when you figure out the occasional less-than-straightforward mission or discover a new mechanic.

Therein lies one of the major problems for me, though. For the most part the missions are fairly routine and don't really require any genuine creativity or problem-solving. You are pretty much handed the tools you need as you need them, and for each obstacle you need to overcome there will be a single tool for the job. As an example: the procedure for bypassing a firewall is to repeatedly type the 'analyze' command until you get the solution, and then to type in that solution - once you have done that once, it is entirely routine. I rarely felt clever solving the missions, and for a game like this I consider that a major failing.

As another reviewer pointed out, there are also elements of the game that seem to be either completely superficial or just unfinished. The best example is the scrubbing of logs, which is quite laborious, but presented at the beginning of the game as a vital measure to cover your tracks. So, the player diligently does so, until inevitably one time they forget, and then DUN DUN DUN...nothing. Apparently this feature is better implemented in the DLC extensions, but I didn't get that far.

Finally, the aspect of the game that ultimately ruined it for me: it is possible to irrevocably break your save game and have no way to recover. If you accidentally delete a file that is mission-critical to the main storyline, and don't notice until the next auto-save (or you save the game yourself), it's game over. This happened to me at about the 4.5 hour mark, and while it certainly wouldn't have taken me that long to get back to the same point from scratch, the game just doesn't work as a rogue-like - I would be going through exactly the same fiddly steps to complete exactly the same routine missions, and I just couldn't face it.

If you want to play a hacking game with a similar aesthetic but some genuine code-based problem-solving, I'd strongly recommend EXAPUNKS, or for an absolutely brilliant command-prompt-based-rogue-like try Duskers.

review_text_raw:
There is no overarching narrative; you're completing puzzles with no purpose. 

Thus, the puzzles are the focus of the game. However, the puzzles are simple and boring. Simple puzzles can still be interesting. Imagine a child's toy where you fit shapes through their respective holes. You can keep yourself busy for a little bit. This game is similar, but everything is a square. How many times can you fit the square in the square hole before it gets boring? Example: you need the password to decrypt a file and you'll find it on the same system within a file called "password.txt". 

Firewall solving requires no input from the player, it's just a timesink. You call the "analyze" command and wait a few seconds at a time until it reveals the answer. You need to call this command multiple times before it starts to reveal the answer - what gameplay function does this serve? Sometimes you don't have any other task to do while the analyze command is processing, so you just wait and wait.. like an idle game. 

Overloading a proxy server involves clicking a button and waiting a few seconds (depending on the number of shells you have up). There's no depth.

Missions share objectives in the form of notes on your computer. For some reason, the devs thought it was a bright idea to have notes take up a significant portion (~30% sometimes) of your memory. So you often have to write up your own abbreviated notes or you won't have enough memory to run the programs you need to crack the ports. The game is fighting itself.

The UI is a mess. A couple hours and your network map becomes an unintelligible mess with no tools to label systems or otherwise organize it. Missions could at least highlight linked servers.

The music is repetitive. Music can make or break a game. In this case, I found myself shutting off music to play my own playlist in the background so I wouldn't be bored to tears while doing all of the waiting the game requires.

review_text_raw:
1. You can't finish all contracts. At some point the game will just tell you "You're good enough for more difficult tasks" and a main quest will trigger, blocking you from accepting new quests. You can never go back and you can't do them after the final mission.

2. You can't create files or directories. Organizing your downloaded files is annoying because you can only use the pre-defined ones. In one contract you're supposed to forge a file, and that works by downloading a file and editing the copy...

3. You can't remove directories. There's almost never a need to do so, but when you need to remove the contents from a directory with multiple subdirectories, you need to access each subdir individually and remove the contents.

4. Autocomplete doesn't add a whitespace after the autocompleteted word. Confusing as hell for a regular terminal user.

5. The final mission consists of multiple phases, which each one explaining your next goal. In phase 3 you're supposed to send a password but you aren't told so. I just used the password I found to login and continued my quest. After a while I got stuck, and after more than an hour I finally looked into a walkthrough - and learnt that I needed to send the password instead of entering it, and that had already solved the final mission by myself over an hour ago. At least I could just click the "complete quest" button 4 times in a row to trigger the ending.

6. The gameplay is quite repetetive. Connect to a server, open the closed ports (which always works the same, for all of them), find the file you need. There are only 2 missions that go beyond that and actually force you to think: The final mission, and the mission before. That doesn't really speak for the game.

7. The map is just plain awful. It's cluttered with nodes from earlier contracts which you never need to connect to anymore. Literally hardest part of the game is finding the correct node on the map.

8. Secrets. Don't get me wrong, secrets are great. But I looked into a guide after finishing the game, and some secrets didn't trigger for me although I definitely satisfied their conditions. So maybe I shouldn't have written "Secrets", but "Bugs". Furthermore, some secrets get you hyped, and when you finally solve their puzzle, you get... a digital clock that even uses up your RAM?

9. Alt+Tab closes the game.

I completed the game in a single session. It was kinda fun, although way too easy. But damn, some of the issues I just mentioned are pissing me off and I'm not going to play the DLC or any user-created mod.

review_text_raw:
Boring and repetitive. It's pretty and has some nice BG music but that's it.

This game is shallow and very restrictive. 
You can't do anything with your rig.
You can't reply to mails during a mission (yeah, it's useless but I expected some minor rôle play elements).
You can only accept one mission at a time.
Once you "change factions" (wtf ?), you can no longer do missions for another even though you still have your credentials.
Many commands don't have a default parameter (mainly those that require a port number) making the process of hacking them annoying.
"Hacking" is better described as running various tools in order to get the server's admin rights then doing what the mission requires ( copy,delete,rename,edit... some file ) and replying to a mail to confirm. You're a "script kiddie" as one of the hackers calls you yet your employers are impressed by your "skills" ... : s

Ok, this game atempts some clever things with the file edit stuff but other than that it's just boring. I want to go further in hopes to see more varied stuff but the post hack stuff is annoying...
All in all, it's a bare bones and simplified version of Interoversion's Uplink for example.

Also, it crashes. Hopefully, the forums explain how to get the XNA beta version that should work on most configs.
